one_liner: 295-line C authoritative DNS demo built on the Nail parser generator; ~2.9x BIND 9.9.5 qps in a 2014 loopback test.
what_it_does: NailDNS is the example authoritative DNS server from the OSDI'14 Nail paper. It reads a zone file, answers UDP queries on 127.0.0.1:53, and exists to show that a grammar-generated parser and serializer can be fast. The DNS wire format and the zone format are declared in a 48-line Nail grammar (examples/dns/dns.nail); the Nail generator emits C structs plus parse_*/gen_* functions, and a 64-line hand-written stream transform handles label compression. It is a standalone program with its own one-line-per-record 'name:TYPE:value' zone format, not a BIND-compatible daemon or a reusable library.
how_it_is_fast: It does very little per packet: one thread in a blocking recvfrom/sendto loop, a per-packet bump-pointer arena (NailArena, 4 KiB blocks, freed in one call), and one lookup in an open-addressing hash table (djb2 hash, linear probing, 1.5x zone-count slots) built once at startup. Parsing and response serialization are generated top-down (PEG-style) C that bounds-checks each read and binds fields straight into plain structs; the paper describes a two-pass design (validate while recording a trace, then bind into the arena). No ACL, view, logging, or DNSSEC work sits on the hot path, and the paper itself only claims Nail's parsers are 'not a barrier to achieving good performance', not that they cause the speedup.
when_to_use: Reproducing or studying the OSDI'14 result: grammar-generated parsing on a small static A-record zone, queried over loopback UDP on one core.
Learning how to express DNS wire format (count fields, label compression via a stream transform) as a declarative grammar that yields both a parser and a serializer.
A throwaway, fast stub responder for load-testing DNS clients in a lab, where the zone is a few MB of lowercase A/NS/CNAME names and RFC corner cases do not matter.
A starting point to copy for a tiny embedded authoritative responder, if you are prepared to fix the known compression and leak bugs yourself.
when_not_to_use: Any production or Internet-facing authoritative service: UDP only, no TCP fallback, never sets TC, no EDNS, no SOA/authority section, no DNSSEC, zone transfer, NOTIFY or TSIG, and the listen address is hard-coded to 127.0.0.1:53.

Untrusted input: the compression-pointer decoder can spin forever (issue #7; AFL-found hangs, fix PR #10 unmerged), generated code has an integer underflow that loops on short input (issue #9), and every malformed packet leaks its arena and output buffer because the error path skips the release calls.
Multi-core throughput: the server is a single blocking recvfrom loop with no threads or sockets sharding.

Real zones: the zone grammar accepts only lowercase a-z and 0-9 in names (no hyphens), only A/NS/MX/CNAME records, not RFC 1035 master-file syntax, and server.c reads at most 4 MiB of zone file (ZONESIZ).
Anything needing a working, maintained toolchain: no commits since 2015, and open issues report the examples fail with 'Syntax error in grammar' and the tests do not compile.

integration.dependencies: Generator: C++11 compiler (Makefile hard-codes clang/clang++), Boost, xxd; example Makefiles also call astyle. Generated C uses libc (malloc/realloc/memset) and setjmp/longjmp despite the README saying it uses no standard library. Server: POSIX sockets and err.h.
integration.min_toolchain: C gnu99 for the examples (generator C parts gnu11), C++11 for the generator; generated code uses GCC/Clang extensions (__builtin_expect, typeof).
integration.platforms: Linux/POSIX UDP (author used Arch and Ubuntu); benchmarked only on x86-64. macOS builds needed the 2015 switch from GNU ld --format=binary to xxd (issue #2).
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the demo server is single-threaded and parsers take caller-owned arenas

gotchas: Name matching is a case-sensitive memcmp plus a djb2 hash over raw bytes, so mixed-case queries (for example DNS 0x20 case randomization) get NXDOMAIN; a name that exists with a different record type also gets NXDOMAIN instead of NODATA.

The decompressor computes pointers as `highbyte & 63 << 8 | ...`, which drops the high 6 offset bits, and it has no loop limit; the paper's 4-hour Metasploit fuzz run did not catch it, but AFL did (PR #10).
MX answers carry only the target name with no 16-bit preference field, and every answer uses a hard-coded 60 s TTL.
The 2015 thesis reports a faster C++-backend NailDNS (median ~190.7K qps), but its BIND column is the identical 2014 data, not a fresh head-to-head run.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Unbound and Hickory DNS are complete DNS servers, and Bundy-DNS's l1cache branch reports a comparable ~4x-over-BIND gain (180K vs 41K qps) from pre-rendered answers. Pick NailDNS only to study or reuse grammar-generated DNS parsing or as a disposable lab responder; for actual serving pick one of those siblings by role.
verified_claims_summary: On one core of an Intel i7-3610QM over loopback, BIND's queryperf (at most 20 outstanding, 60 s, 7 runs each, April 2014, 0 lost queries) against a 50,000-name A-record zone with ~10% NXDOMAIN gave a median 139,215 qps for NailDNS vs 47,235 qps for BIND 9.9.5 (~2.9x), and mean RTT 0.139 ms vs 0.416 ms. NailDNS was built with -std=gnu99 -O3 on an unnamed compiler; BIND's build flags, thread count and named.conf are not published.
status_note: Abandoned since 2015-08-17 with the compression-hang fix (PR #10) unmerged since 2020; MIT-licensed and small enough to copy, but expect to repair the build and the DNS-compression code yourself.
